config.title: Child processes

intro.title: Child processes
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Node.js application that uses child processes to run external commands, like listing directory contents, from within your JavaScript code. You will learn the core concept of spawning separate processes to execute system commands or other scripts, allowing your main program to continue running or handle the output. The main technologies involved are the Node.js `child_process` module and its methods such as `exec`. By the end, you'll understand how to safely run and interact with external processes in a Node.js environment.
intro.usecase: Child processes are essential in Node.js for offloading heavy tasks to keep your main application responsive. For example, a web dashboard that processes large CSV uploads or generates PDF reports uses child processes to run these intensive operations in the background. This pattern also powers features like real-time data processing in analytics tools or executing system commands in DevOps automation scripts, ensuring the primary UI remains fast and interactive.

objectives: Initialize a child process using the spawn method
Configure child process options for standard I/O streams
Manipulate child process output by handling data events
Control child process execution by managing process lifecycle
Integrate error handling for child process failures
Apply the exec method for simpler command execution
Construct a script that communicates between parent and child processes

steps.title: Import the child_process module
steps.instruction: Import the child_process module using require() to make its functionality available in your script.
steps.hint: Use the require() function with the module name 'child_process' and assign it to a variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing another core module
const fs = require('fs');
steps.expectedOutcome: The child_process module is imported and ready to use.
successCriteria: The child_process module is imported using require() and assigned to a variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using require() with the exact module name 'child_process' and assigning it to a variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to use require('child_process') and assign it to a variable so you can use it later.

steps.title: Create a basic exec function call
steps.instruction: Create a function named runCommand that uses child_process.exec() to execute the shell command 'ls' (or 'dir' on Windows) and logs the result to the console.
steps.hint: Use the exec method from the child_process module you imported. The function should take no arguments and call exec with a command string and a callback.
steps.seedCode:
const { exec } = require('child_process');

// Create a function named runCommand that uses exec to run 'ls' and logs the output
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named runCommand is defined that will execute 'ls' and log the output when called.
successCriteria: The runCommand function is defined, uses exec with the command 'ls' (or 'dir'), and includes a callback that logs the stdout.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named runCommand, uses exec with 'ls' (or 'dir'), and logs the output in the callback.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't meet the requirements. Check that you're using exec from child_process, the command is 'ls' (or 'dir'), and you're logging the output.

steps.title: Handle exec callback with error and output
steps.instruction: Inside the runCommand function, update the exec callback to check for errors and log stdout or stderr appropriately.
steps.hint: The exec callback receives three parameters: error, stdout, and stderr. Use an if statement to handle errors first.
steps.expectedOutcome: The runCommand function will now properly handle errors and log the command output or error messages.
successCriteria: The exec callback includes an if statement checking for errors and logs stdout when successful or stderr when there's an error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking for errors first in the callback and logging both stdout and stderr appropriately.
steps.feedbackWrong: The callback should handle both success and error cases. Remember to check if error exists and log stderr when there's an error, otherwise log stdout.

steps.title: Create a spawn process for streaming data
steps.instruction: Create a new function named spawnProcess that uses child_process.spawn() to run the command 'find . -name "*.js"'.
steps.hint: Use the spawn function imported from child_process. The first argument is the command, the second is an array of arguments.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a new function named spawnProcess that uses spawn to run a find command.
successCriteria: The spawnProcess function is defined and uses spawn with the command 'find . -name "*.js"'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using spawn (not exec) and the command 'find . -name "*.js"'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. Remember to use spawn from child_process and run the find command with the correct arguments.

steps.title: Handle spawn stdout and stderr events
steps.instruction: Inside the spawnProcess function, set up event listeners on the spawned process to handle 'data' events from stdout and stderr streams.
steps.hint: Use the .on() method on process.stdout and process.stderr to listen for 'data' events and log the received data.
steps.expectedOutcome: The spawnProcess function will now log data chunks as they arrive from the spawned process's stdout and stderr streams.
successCriteria: The spawnProcess function contains event listeners for 'data' events on both process.stdout and process.stderr that log the received data.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added event listeners for both stdout and stderr streams.
steps.feedbackWrong: The event listeners for stdout and stderr data events are not properly set up. Check the hint for guidance.

steps.title: Handle spawn exit and error events
steps.instruction: Inside the spawnProcess function, add event listeners for the 'exit', 'error', and 'close' events on the spawned process to handle completion and errors.
steps.hint: Use process.on('eventName', callback) to listen for each event. For 'exit', log the exit code. For 'error', log the error. For 'close', log that the process closed.
steps.expectedOutcome: The spawnProcess function will now handle the full lifecycle of the spawned process, including completion and errors.
successCriteria: The spawnProcess function includes event listeners for 'exit', 'error', and 'close' events on the spawned process.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some event listeners, but make sure to include all three: 'exit', 'error', and 'close'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires adding event listeners for 'exit', 'error', and 'close' events on the spawned process. Check the hint for guidance.

steps.title: Pass arguments to a spawned process
steps.instruction: Modify the spawn call in your spawnProcess function to pass arguments to the 'ls' command. Pass an array as the second argument with the flags '-l' and '-a'.
steps.hint: The spawn function can take an array of arguments as its second parameter. For example: spawn('ls', ['-l', '-a'])
steps.expectedOutcome: The spawn call now includes command-line arguments, making the child process execute 'ls -l -a'.
successCriteria: The spawn function is called with two arguments: the command 'ls' and an array containing '-l' and '-a'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you're passing the arguments correctly. The spawn function should take the command as the first argument and an array of arguments as the second.
steps.feedbackWrong: The spawn call should include both the command and an array of arguments. Try modifying it to: spawn('ls', ['-l', '-a'])

steps.title: Use execFile for executing files directly
steps.instruction: Create a new function named runExecFile that uses child_process.execFile() to execute the 'ls' command directly.
steps.hint: The execFile function is similar to exec but executes a file directly without a shell by default. Use the same callback pattern with error, stdout, and stderr parameters.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new function named runExecFile is added to the code, using execFile to execute 'ls' with a callback that handles error, stdout, and stderr.
successCriteria: The runExecFile function is defined, uses execFile with 'ls' as the first argument, and includes a callback function with error, stdout, and stderr parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your runExecFile function uses execFile with 'ls' and includes a callback with error, stdout, and stderr parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The runExecFile function is missing or doesn't use execFile correctly. Remember to create a function named runExecFile that calls execFile('ls', callback).

steps.title: Create a fork for Node.js module processes
steps.instruction: Create a new function named forkProcess that uses child_process.fork() to run another Node.js module as a separate process.
steps.hint: Use the fork() method from the child_process module you imported earlier. The fork() method takes a module path as its first argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new function named forkProcess is created that uses the fork() method to create a child process.
successCriteria: The forkProcess function is defined and uses child_process.fork() with a module path argument.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the fork() method from the child_process module and passing a module path as an argument.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function wasn't created correctly. Remember to use child_process.fork() to create a child process that can run another Node.js module.

steps.title: Send and receive messages between forked processes
steps.instruction: Inside the forkProcess function, set up message passing by adding a 'message' event listener to the forked child process and using send() to send a message from the parent.
steps.hint: Use child.on('message', callback) to listen for messages from the child, and child.send(message) to send a message from the parent.
steps.expectedOutcome: The forkProcess function will now be able to communicate with the child process via IPC, listening for incoming messages and sending an initial message.
successCriteria: The forkProcess function includes a 'message' event listener on the child process and uses child.send() to send a message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've made progress, but ensure you've added both the 'message' event listener and the send() call inside forkProcess.
steps.feedbackWrong: The forkProcess function doesn't yet include the required IPC setup. Review the hint and analogous example.
